Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'fall into emptiness,' but in these records the observable warning is against falling into a blank nothing. The term occurs 325 times in 128 allowed texts; the expanded form 'fall into blank annihilation' (落空亡) occurs 63 times in 37 texts. Dahui reports people who hear 'a teaching in which nothing is obtained' (無所得法) and become afraid that they will fall into blankness; he answers by asking whether the very one who fears falling into blankness is empty. A lamp dialogue answers the charge that Chan teachers mostly fall into blankness by saying that letters and other things arise from wisdom and that, when 'great function appears before one' (大用現前), there can be no falling into blankness. Another exchange dismantles the spatial wording itself: asked whether 'originally there is nothing' falls into blankness, the reply asks, 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立). The same collection says that people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). There are 37 occurrences of 'not fall into blankness' (不落空) and 21 of the warning 'do not fall into blankness' (莫落空).
Senses.Note: The translation 'blankness' follows the records' direct corrections: 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立), and 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). The entry records the corpus's accusations, warnings, and replies.

Occurrences.Kwic: 纔聞善知識說無所得法。便心裏疑惑。怕落空去。妙喜每見如此說者。即問他。只這怕落空者。還空也無。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui describes the fear and responds by questioning whether the one who fears falling into blankness is itself empty.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古德喚作落空亡外道魂不散死人。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui cites an older description: 'an outsider fallen into blank annihilation, a dead person whose ghost has not dispersed.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 有律師法明。謂師曰。禪師家多落空。師曰。却是坐主家多落空。法明大驚曰。何得落空。師曰。經論是紙墨文字。紙墨文字者俱空。設於聲上建立名句等法。無非是空。坐主執滯教體。豈不落空。法明曰。禪師落空否。師曰。不落空。曰何却不落空。師曰。文字等皆從智慧而生。大用現前那得落空。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of the Transmission of the Lamp. The exchange turns the accusation back and says that letters arise from wisdom, so great function appearing before one does not fall into blankness; the two-speaker occurrence remains unkeyed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰本來無莫落空否。師曰。空既是無墮從何立。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct exchange rejects the premise: if blankness is absent, no falling can be established.

Occurrences.Kwic: 人不敢忘心。是恐落空無撈摸處。不知空本無空唯一真界耳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text says people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says that blankness itself is originally not blank.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, the 'place where something falls.' The term occurs 2,117 times in 310 allowed texts. Chan records apply it to words, answers, cases, actions, people, and one's life: 'know where it lands' (知落處) occurs 770 times in 205 texts, while 'not know where it lands' (不知落處) occurs 172 times in 89 texts. Yuanwu says that as soon as Danxia raised it, he knew where it landed (才方舉起便知落處), and his Blue Cliff prose twice contrasts knowing and not knowing where Mazu's public case lands. Dahui asks whether the assembly knows where his teacher's words land and says that knowing it identifies the top graduate (還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元). Changqing asks a monk, 'Do you understand where it lands?' (還委落處麼). A lamp record joins origin and destination: 'if you know where it arises, then you know where life lands' (若知起處。便知身命落處). Xiuyelin gives the richest explicit relation found: 'the fundamental matter is precisely where the person's own life-source lands' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). The article therefore keeps the verbal image and reports what the texts assign a landing point; it does not replace that image with an imported abstraction.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas and obvious variants were searched. No formula directly defines the bare headword. The Xiuyelin sentence instead defines the fundamental matter by means of it and is retained as the strongest relational witness. Questions about knowing, not knowing, and asking where something lands form one broad corpus-wide family rather than master-specific senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiuyelin's instruction to Layman Pan directly identifies the fundamental matter as where the person's own life-source lands. No exact roster link was assigned.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此箇公案。若知落處便獨步丹霄。若不知落處。往往枯木巖前差路去在。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's Blue Cliff prose comments on Mazu's sun-face buddha and moon-face buddha case, explicitly contrasting knowing and not knowing where the case lands.
In Yuanwu's sixth volume of assembly addresses, Yuanwu says that Danxia knew where it landed as soon as it was raised.

Occurrences.Kwic: 敢問諸人還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui asks the assembly whether they know where his teacher's words land and states the consequence in his own assembly address.
Five Lamps Compendium, Changqing Huileng section. Changqing asks a monk whether he understands where it lands; the short dialogue remains unlinked because no roster spelling was asserted.

Occurrences.Kwic: 若知起處。便知身命落處。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Five Lamps Compendium, Emperor Taizong section. A teacher links knowing where thunder arises with knowing where life lands; the emperor is the section subject, not the speaker.
